title: Containers, pods, deployments
bridge: A Kubernetes Deployment is like `npm start` on many machines at once. Except the machines are disposable. A pod can die at any moment, and a new one starts with a new name and IP. You never ssh in to restart anything.
intro: Our agent services do not run on a VM you log in to. The LLM gateway, the broker, the orchestrator worker, the Slack app and Temporal run as pods on inf-rhinohealth. That is a Kubernetes cluster DevOps already operates. This lesson gives you the five words you need to read and write what goes there.

picture.caption: You describe what you want; the control plane keeps it true, even when a pod dies.

sections.h: Start from one container on your laptop
p: In p1-8 you built a Docker image for a Node service and ran it with `docker run`. A running image is a container: one process tree with its own filesystem and network.

Kubernetes runs the same images, but it never runs a bare container. It runs a pod: one or more containers that share one IP address and can talk over localhost. Almost all of our pods hold exactly one container.
The rest of this lesson is about what sits around the pod. Who starts it, who restarts it, and how other pods find it.
sections.because: We pull the image first to see the two ways to name it. A tag can move; a digest cannot.

code.text:
docker pull nginx:1.27
docker image inspect nginx:1.27 --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'
# nginx@sha256:3f1c…   <- the digest: the exact bytes, forever

docker run --rm -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost:8080
docker rm -f web

notes.text: A tag like 1.27 is a label. Whoever owns the image can point it at new bytes tomorrow.
A digest is the sha256 of the image content. Our Terraform units pin images by digest for this reason.
This is one container on one machine. A pod is the same thing with a Kubernetes wrapper around it.
On your laptop you clean up by hand. In Kubernetes, something else restarts what you remove.

p: A cluster is a set of machines (nodes) plus a control plane. The control plane is the API that stores what you asked for and makes the nodes match it. You talk to it with the `kubectl` command.

inf-rhinohealth is our internal cluster: Amazon EKS 1.36 in the infrastructure account (123456789012), region us-east-1. Karpenter adds and removes Spot nodes as pods come and go, so a node is as disposable as a pod.

The internal tools already live there: Vault, n8n, Nexus, Teleport, VictoriaMetrics and the GitHub Actions runner sets. Our agent services join them. They are the LLM gateway (G0-15), the broker, the orchestrator worker and the Slack app (G3-17). Then the agents' Temporal (G3-06) and the brain bot (G6-22).

Two things to remember about inf. It is not a product cluster, so nothing there is deployed by Argo CD. Everything is a Terraform `helm_release` unit in the infrastructure repo (next lesson). And KEDA is off, so replica counts are fixed numbers.

callout.text: The sandbox VMs where agents work are NOT on this cluster. They are EC2 machines in the separate ai-agents account. Only the services that hold credentials run on inf.

sections.h: Pods die; a Deployment keeps the count
p: A pod is never repaired. When its node goes away or its process crashes, the pod is gone. What you create is a Deployment: it says which image to run and how many copies (replicas) you want.
The Deployment watches the count. Two pods wanted, one alive: it starts another one, with a new random name and a new IP. This is why you never write a pod's name or IP anywhere.

Below is the shape of the Deployment that our shared chart (modules/ai-agents-service, from G0-15) renders for the broker. Read it once with the notes; you will see it again rendered by `helm template`.
sections.because: We write the Deployment, not the pod, so the cluster can replace pods for us without anyone being paged.

code.file: what modules/ai-agents-service renders for the broker (shortened)
code.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: broker
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  replicas: 2                 # fixed: KEDA is off on inf
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: broker }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: broker }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: broker
          image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/ai-agents-broker@sha256:…
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 } }
          securityContext:
            runAsUser: 10001
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            capabilities: { drop: [ALL] }

notes.text: Two copies. If one dies the Deployment starts another; if a node is drained, both move.
The selector says which pods belong to this Deployment: the ones with the label app=broker.
Everything under template is the pod recipe. Each new pod is stamped from it.
The image from inf ECR, pinned by digest, as G3-17 asks. A tag could change under us; a digest cannot.
The readiness probe calls GET /health. A pod gets traffic only after this returns 200.
Non-root user, read-only root filesystem, no capabilities: the same flags Byte uses for its broker container.

sections.h: A Service is the stable name in front
p: Pods come and go, so other pods need a name that stays. A Service is that name. It picks the pods by label and spreads calls over the live ones.

Inside the cluster the name is DNS: `broker.ai-agents.svc.cluster.local`, or `broker.ai-agents` for short. Type ClusterIP means the name works only inside the cluster. That is what we want for the broker's internal port: nothing outside inf should reach it.
sections.because: The orchestrator must call the broker by a name that survives every pod restart.

code.file: the Service next to the Deployment
code.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: broker
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector: { app: broker }
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 8080
      targetPort: 8080

notes.text: The DNS name other pods use: broker.ai-agents.
ClusterIP: reachable inside the cluster only. Our UIs get an HTTPRoute on envoy-internal instead; that is a separate object.
The same label as the Deployment's pods. That is the whole link between them.
The port callers use. targetPort is the port the container listens on; here they match.

p: A namespace is a folder for objects. Names must be unique inside it, and most access rules are written per namespace. Our agent services share one namespace, `ai-agents`; the OTel collector has `otel-collector`; the runner sets have their own.
The namespace is also the unit that network policy (lesson p5-4) reasons about. 'Only pods in ai-agents may reach Temporal on port 7233' is a sentence about a namespace.
Do not confuse the Kubernetes namespace `ai-agents` with the Temporal namespace `ai-agents` (G3-06). Same word, two systems: one groups pods, the other groups workflows.

sections.h: The kubectl you will use every week
p: You will mostly read, not write: the YAML comes from Terraform and Helm. These are the commands that answer 'is it running and why not'.
Every command takes `-n <namespace>`. Without it you are looking at the `default` namespace, which is empty, and you will think your pods are gone.
sections.because: Reading pod state is how you check that a deploy worked and how you find a crash.

code.text:
kubectl config current-context          # ALWAYS first. prod-rhinohealth? stop.
kubectl get pods -n ai-agents             # names, READY, STATUS, RESTARTS
kubectl describe pod -n ai-agents broker-7d9c6f8b5c-k2xq9   # events: why it is Pending or crashing
kubectl logs -n ai-agents deploy/broker --tail=50            # stdout of the broker's pods
kubectl get svc,deploy -n ai-agents       # Services and Deployments in one list
kubectl rollout status -n ai-agents deploy/broker           # waits until new pods are ready

notes.text: Your laptop's kubectl context may point at prod-rhinohealth. Check before every command; add --context kind-academy in the lab.
STATUS Running and READY 1/1 is good. CrashLoopBackOff means the process exits; ImagePullBackOff means the digest or ECR access is wrong.
The Events section at the bottom is where Kubernetes explains itself.
deploy/broker means 'any pod of that Deployment'. You do not need the random pod name.

callout.text: On your laptop, run kubectl only against the kind cluster you create in the lab. Never against prod-rhinohealth or inf-rhinohealth from a lesson. Changes to inf go through a Terraform PR that a person applies.

lab.faded: Do the same for a second Deployment called orchestrator with 1 replica of the same image, in the same namespace. Then delete its only pod and watch it come back. The last step, exposing it as a Service and calling it from a probe pod, is yours: write the two commands yourself.
lab.alone: Create a namespace called otel-collector and a Deployment called collector with 3 replicas of nginx:1.27. Scale it down to 1 with `kubectl -n otel-collector scale deployment collector --replicas=1`. Before you run scale, write down which two pods you expect to disappear and which name survives. Then check. Keep the cluster: p5-2 to p5-4 reuse it. Delete it at the end with `kind delete cluster --name academy`.
lab.done: You deleted a pod by name and the Deployment replaced it with a new name and IP. A probe pod reached it through the Service name.

quiz.q: The broker pod broker-7d9c6f8b5c-k2xq9 is crashing. What do you do?

options.text: ssh to the node, fix the config, and restart the process
options.why: There is no ssh and no fixing in place. Pods are replaced, never repaired.

options.text: Read `kubectl describe pod` and `kubectl logs`, fix the image or config in the Terraform unit, and let a person apply it
options.why: The pod recipe lives in the Deployment, which Terraform owns. You change the recipe, not the pod.

options.text: Delete the pod so the Deployment starts a clean one
options.why: The new pod runs the same recipe and will crash the same way. Deleting only hides the problem for a minute.

quiz.q: The orchestrator needs to call the broker. Which address goes in its config?

options.text: The pod IP 10.244.0.6 from `kubectl get pods -o wide`
options.why: That IP belongs to one pod and dies with it. The next pod gets another IP.
Pod names are random and change on every restart.
The Service is the stable DNS name and sends each call to a live pod.

quiz.q: Why does the Deployment pin the broker image by digest and not by the tag 0.1.0?

options.text: Tags are slower to pull than digests
options.why: Pull speed is the same. The difference is what the name means.

options.text: A tag can be moved to new bytes later; a digest names exactly one image forever
options.why: A digest is a hash of the content. G3-17 asks for digests so nobody can swap what runs under a known name.
ECR supports both. Our ECR repos even set tags_immutability_enabled, but a digest is still the stronger pin.

words.plain: A running image: one process tree with its own filesystem and network, like `docker run` gives you.
The smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers sharing one IP; it is replaced, never repaired.
An object that says which image to run and how many pods to keep, and replaces pods that die.
A stable DNS name that sends calls to whichever pods currently match its label.
A folder for objects in the cluster; our agent services share the one called ai-agents.
The cluster's API: it stores what you asked for and makes the nodes match it.
Our internal EKS cluster in the infrastructure account where the tools and the agent services run.

tickets.why: The gateway is the first agent service deployed on inf; you now know what its Deployment, Service and probe mean.
Deploys the broker, orchestrator worker and Slack app as pods in the ai-agents namespace with fixed replicas and pinned digests.
Temporal's chart renders Deployments and Services like the ones here; its frontend stays ClusterIP.
The brain bot is a one-replica Deployment with no Service, because Socket Mode dials out.

remember: You describe a Deployment and a Service; the cluster keeps the pods alive and the name stable. Never write down a pod's name or IP.
